summary: Kaieteur Airport is a remote airstrip located within Kaieteur National Park in the interior of Guyana, serving as the primary air access point for visitors to Kaieteur Falls, one of the world's tallest single-drop waterfalls at 226 meters. The airport primarily handles small charter and tourist flights, as the surrounding Potaro Plateau and dense rainforest make overland access extremely difficult. Its isolated location offers arriving passengers an immediate immersion into one of South America's most pristine wilderness areas.
faqs:
Q: How do I get to Kaieteur Airport?
A: The airport is only accessible by air, with no road connections. Most visitors arrive on small charter flights from Georgetown's Ogle Airport, with flight times of approximately 1 to 1.5 hours over the rainforest.

Q: What airlines serve Kaieteur Airport?
A: Scheduled service is limited; most flights are operated by charter companies and local operators such as Roraima Airways and Trans Guyana Airways, often as part of packaged tour itineraries.

Q: Are there facilities at the airport?
A: Facilities are very basic, consisting of a small terminal building. There are no ATMs, shops, or car rental services. The airport exists primarily to serve park visitors rather than as a commercial hub.

Q: Do I need a permit or guide to visit Kaieteur Falls?
A: Yes, all visitors must enter through Kaieteur National Park and typically must be accompanied by a licensed park guide. Tour packages generally arrange permits, transportation, and guided walks in advance.
transport_tips: All transport to and from the airport is coordinated through tour operators or charter companies, as there is no public transit or road access to the surrounding park. Charter flights should be booked well in advance, especially during the dry season (September to November) when weather conditions are most favorable. Upon landing, visitors are typically transferred directly to the park lodge or trailheads via guided arrangement rather than independent transport.
local_tip: Visit during the early morning hours when the falls are most likely to produce rainbows from the mist, and consider a side flight over the falls for an aerial perspective—pilots often circle the drop on approach, and many charter operators will arrange this on request for an unforgettable view of the full 226-meter cascade.
